entry.title: The Unheard Voices in STEM
entry.content:
One of the most engaging classes I’ve taken in all of my undergraduate years was actually this past semester, when I took BIOL 259: Applied Population Biology, as part of my Computational Biology major.

Aside from our small classroom size of 11 students, it wasn’t anything special. Most of our content revolved around population modeling of species, and computational tools & techniques for population-based research. Yet, the most fascinating portion of the class wasn’t even related to any of those, but rather our last module on Human Dimensions, which basically covered the impacts of colonialism, racism and other social inequalities on science to help inform more justice-centered research.

The module consisted of three unique topics:

  1. Biological Impact of Social Inequities
  2. Decolonizing Science
  3. Indigenous Knowledge

Rather than simply being lectured on the content, each group had to present the content in a unique & informative way. Our group picked topic #3, and we made a case study inspired by the Onondaga Lake in Central New York near our school. Here, we split the class into two groups, one representing an indigenous population, and the other representing researchers tasked with cleaning up the lake. We had each group come up with a solution to clean up the lake and then had the two groups come together to discuss and find a unified solution. Ironically, the more talkative group ended up being the scientists and served as a unique, albeit unintentional reflection of how researchers often diminish the voices of the indigenous community in their field work.

As biologists, medical experts, or even just scientists of any kind, we focus so much on finer details and concepts like pathways, gene sequences, and cellular functions, that we can sometimes forget the broader context that our work lives in. Science doesn’t only happen in isolation, it also occurs within communities, history and power structures.

Our topic discussion that Wednesday reminded me that representation in science isn’t just about who’s in the lab, but also the voices that are present and heard in the room when decisions are made. If science and medicine are meant to serve society, then it has to be built with the people it affects.

entry.title: My Neurodiverse Superpower
entry.content:
I think in many ways, I’ve always functioned outside of systems, yet it’s ironic that I spend so much time trying to understand how they work. I tend to intellectualize everything from human connection, relationships, and behavioral patterns, almost like I need to understand them before I’m allowed to participate in them. For a long time, I assumed that as a personal crack, like a puzzle I was trying to solve but could never quite fit the pieces properly. Learning that I’m autistic and have ADHD has helped me a lot in learning to accept parts of myself and understand my own needs & boundaries. Having language to explain who I am has helped me reframe my experience from an emotional deficit to a different & more unique way of thinking.

This shift has changed how I approach my future goals as a scientist, and the way I see myself in STEM. For a biology major, it’s quite ironic that I always struggled with memorizing mountains of content, often misplacing cell systems or not being able to remember the right vocabulary for certain physiological processes. Yet, my second major, data science, has really helped me to hone into my neurological strengths. Hyperfixation, which I once thought of as a curse to lift, has instead become a magical ability that I can harness in learning to analyze data, find patterns, and craft unique narratives just out of a large sequence of numbers or words. It’s helped me to recognize the aspects of biology that I do enjoy, mainly more quantitative domains such as genomics & population genetics, which often emphasize problem solving more than reciting the steps of the Krebs cycle. And working with data has helped me to harness and develop my abilities to pick up new skills, from different bioinformatics softwares to machine learning and NLP packages that I would have never expected to learn years ago. These traits don’t always align with traditional academic metrics, but they are essential in science, where progress often comes from questioning assumptions and noticing what others overlook.

As I think about my future in science, I’ve come to believe that neurodiversity isn’t just something to accommodate, but something to value. Our world often treats difference as something to smooth out, rather than something to design around. But science advances because of people who think differently and challenge existing systems while still caring deeply about how they function. If we create environments that support multiple ways of thinking, rather than rewarding only one, we don’t just help neurodivergent people succeed, we also build a more thoughtful, innovative, and humane future for science and society as a whole.

entry.title: Bridging the Gap Between AI/ML, Healthcare and Social Justice

link.title: Bridging the Gap Between AI/ML, Healthcare and Social Justice

entry.content:
One of the most interesting and personal talks I attended at the 2024 Out in STEM Conference in Portland, Oregon was An Introduction to AI/ML Healthcare Solutions, Including the Ongoing Need for Bringing LGBTQ+ Communities Into the Fold. It was really enlightening but also telling to see how these fields overlap with queer rights and social justice while bringing attention to the need for representation in biomedical diagnostics & decision-making.

At its best, AI and machine learning have enormous potential in medicine: improving diagnostic accuracy, identifying disease risk earlier, optimizing treatment strategies, and scaling healthcare access in ways that were previously impossible. From radiology and pathology to genomics and electronic health records, AI systems are already shaping how care is delivered. Much of the excitement around these tools comes from their promise of objectivity and replacing human inconsistency with data-driven insight.

Yet as AI advancements are rising, with numerous applications in fields like finance, education, security, and of course, medicine, it’s important to understand that machines do not operate in a vacuum; they are just as much susceptible to reproducing, and sometimes amplifying, the very biases and structural disparities they are often assumed to eliminate.

In healthcare, these issues carry particularly high stakes. When LGBTQ+ individuals, racial minorities, disabled people, or other marginalized communities are underrepresented or misrepresented in training data, AI models may systematically underperform for those populations. This can manifest in missed diagnoses, inaccurate risk predictions, or exclusion from downstream clinical decision-making. What appears to be a technical limitation is often a reflection of deeper social inequities embedded in how data are collected, labeled, and interpreted.

This is where the intersection of AI, healthcare, and social justice becomes not just relevant, but necessary. Building better models isn’t only about improving accuracy or efficiency, but also about asking who these systems are designed for, whose data are being used, and who benefits from their deployment. It requires interdisciplinary collaboration across computer science, biology, public health, ethics, and policy, as well as meaningful engagement with the communities most affected by these technologies.

For me, this talk reinforced why I’m drawn to research that sits at the boundary between computational methods and social context. Whether working with machine learning models, genomic data, or population-scale health studies, I’ve become increasingly interested in how we move from technical innovation to responsible action. If AI is going to shape the future of medicine, it must be built with intention and grounded in equity, transparency, and an awareness of the social systems it inevitably reflects.
